content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is ultimately concerned with the use of autoencoder methods in unsupervised outlier detection, in which reconstruction error is used as the measure of outlierness. The authors claim that such methods tend to detect points in directions associated with poorly-recovered principal components, while often ignoring candidates in the directions of well-recovered components. To cope with this, they propose that complete reconstruction be inhibited through an eigenvalue regularization, so as to encourage a more even discovery of outliers over all principal components directions.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1) Theoretical arguments (Sections 3.1 and 3.2) showing the effect of suppressing complete reconstruction. Under the assumption that the data follows a multivariate Gaussian distribution, the authors analyze the relationship between reconstruction error and Mahalanobis distance, showing that they relate by a factor equal to the square of the difference of the roots of true vs learned eigenvalues. The implication here is that complete learning of the true eigenvalue would result in no outliers being detected along the associated principal component direction. Although the authors did not explicitly say so, arguments based on eigenvector decomposition are appropriate given that autoencoder-based learning converges to PCA. 

2) A strategy for regularizing the root eigenvalue difference so to prevent complete reconstruction along each component direction. The effect of the regularization is to spread the detection of outliers more evenly across the component directions.

Weaknesses:

1) The empirical justification is not sufficient. Several experiments are performed on synthetic datasets with Gaussian-distributed coordinates; due to the properties of autoencoder-based outlier detection, it is hardly surprising that they would support the theoretical arguments. Although one experiment was performed on real data, there was no firm notion of outlierness provided, nor was a ground-truth outlier set provided. More seriously, there seemed to be no testing against existing ground truth outlier data sets (e.g. those made available online by Campos et al., "On the evaluation of unsupervised outlier detection: measures, datasets, and an empirical study", DAMI 30, 891-927 (2016)). The potential impact of the proposed reconstruction suppression strategy is still unclear.

2) The arguments and analysis are undercut by dubious assumptions and a lack of mathematical crispness. For example, the authors claim that "most datasets follow a multidimensional Gaussian distribution" instead of recognizing the implicit assumptions underlying the use of autoencoders for outlier detection, due to their known convergence to PCA. Another example is the assumption that estimates of a coordinate value increase monotonically with the input value - although the tendency is there, monotonicity is not guaranteed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Although the paper is generally well-organized and readable, there are numerous presentational flaws: typesetting issues, strange idioms, erroneous assertions, and (in Figure 1) text descriptions that do not always match the point configurations shown.

Despite the abovementioned issues regarding empirical evaluation, the synthetic experimentation is largely reproduceable. The authors do include in the supplementary material some additional discussion of the regularization parameter and how it can be set in practice.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the authors have made reasonable arguments for their strategy of autoencoder-based outlier detection through reconstruction suppression, the empirical evidence is insufficient to establish whether the stragety would have practical impact.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors provide an eigenvalue-based analysis of the autoencoders for outlier detection. Based on the eigenvalue differences between input and output, a regularization term has been proposed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Unfortunately, the paper does not make a clear presentation to deliver the ideas. The definition of the high-leverage points and influential points are vague, and the settings from which the analysis and the proposed algorithm have been motivated are unclear. In particular, the authors use Gaussian, linear projection, and eigenvalue analysis. Why don’t the authors use a simple PCA?

In the regularization term, do the authors assume that the $k$-th component in the input will be transferred to the same $k$-th component of the output? This does not make sense.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Many parts of the paper show unclear explanation, and the terms are used without definition.
For example the following terms in page 3: “intrinsic information”, “poorly recovered principal component”, “better recovered principal component”, and the terms in page 4: “Covariance matrix off-diagonal”, “intrinsic dimension”, and “actual dimension” if I name a few, have been used without definition.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is unclear and does not show any analysis that can reach the threshold of the acceptance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on improving the outlier detection performance, especially the detection on the high leverage points (HLP). To achieve this goal, the authors leverage the autoencoder and propose a new loss function for the autoencoder. To evaluate the proposed method, the authors have conducted experiments on both synthetic and real datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1) The authors provide theoretical analysis as well as empirical evaluation.
2) The authors have conducted experiments on both synthetic and real datasets.


Weakness:
1) MSE is known to be sensitive to outliers. Thus, when people use autoencoder for outlier detection, people typically use a robust loss function such as L1 loss. So, why should we worry about MSE-autoencoder if we already have other robust autoencoders?

2) I think the comparisons are not fair. The authors only compare their method with MSE-autoencoder which is known not to work well. The authors should compare their method with other robust autoencoder models such as in ref1 and ref2:

Ref1: Lai, Chieh-Hsin, Dongmian Zou, and Gilad Lerman. "Novelty detection via robust variational autoencoding." arXiv preprint arXiv:2006.05534 (2020).

Ref2: Li, Taihui, et al. "Rethink Autoencoders: Robust Manifold Learning."

3) The evaluation metrics may be problematic. As AUC (area under curve) may yield misleading conclusions when the data is imbalanced. Thus I suggest the authors should also evaluate the performance using other metrics.
 
4) How to choose/decide the proper numbers/hyper-parameters for the two loss terms?


5) For the real dataset, it is a relatively low-dimensional dataset, how does the proposed method work on real-world, high-dimensional, and more complex datasets? Will the observations still be held?

6) Minor issues: there are some typos in the word “complete”.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The overall presentation looks good. No code is provided. Although the general training setting has been mentioned in the paper, it is not quite sure whether the results can be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although this paper has some strengths such as having theoretical analysis in addition to empirical evaluation, there are several concerns as I list in the [Strength And Weaknesses] part, which significantly degrade its quality.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of detecting High Leverage Points (HLP) outliers in autoencoder-based outlier detection. HLP is a type of outlier that is well reconstructed when fed into an autoencoder. In the mathematical analysis presented in the paper, the authors argue that the detection of HLP is impossible, or at least difficult, when an autoencoder is able to exactly reconstruct some of in-distribution samples. To facilitate the detection of HLP, the authors propose a new regularizor that inhibits the complete reconstruction of inliers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Streanths

* The paper addresses the problem of autoencoders unexpectedly reconstructing outliers, which is an important and relevant issue in the machine learning community given the wide use of autoencoders in practice.

# Weaknesses

* (Novelty) The phenomenon of an outlier being reconstructed by an autoencoder is well-known in previous literature. In fact, some works have addressed this issue directly, but this paper does not cite them. The authors need to discuss the advantages of the proposed approach over these works and also need to provide empirical comparisons. A few examples of relevant literature that is missing in this paper are:
    * Zhou, Yibo. "Rethinking Reconstruction Autoencoder-Based Out-of-Distribution Detection." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2022.
    * Yoon, Sangwoong, Yung-Kyun Noh, and Frank Park. "Autoencoding under normalization constraints." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021.
    * Gong, Dong, et al. "Memorizing normality to detect anomaly: Memory-augmented deep autoencoder for unsupervised anomaly detection." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2019.

* (Clarity) The clarity of the paper needs to be significantly improved. Since HLP and Influential Point (IP) are central concepts in this paper, the terms need to be defined precisely with mathematical representation, possibly in Section 3. However currently, these terms are only loosely defined. Also, explicitly stating the definition of outlier can improve the clarity of the paper, as there may be a few different ways to mathematically characterize an outlier.

* (Quality / Significance) The Gaussian assumption (Assumption 1) used throughout the paper is not quite acceptable in modern machine learning settings. I believe most of the contemporary machine learning algorithms deal with non-Gaussian data and it is not a good idea to build an algorithm based on Gaussian assumption.

* (Quality / Significance) The proposed algorithm is built based on a view that "autoencoders will focus on recovering the principal components of a dataset eventually" (Page 4). This statement is only true when a linear autoencoder is used.

* (Quality / Significance) The scale of empirical experiments is very small and not enough to convince readers to think that this algorithm would work competitively in practice.

* (Reproducibility) It is not very clear that how the eigenvalues used in the proposed regularizor are computed.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the paper tries to investigate an important phenomenon of outlier reconstruction in autoencoders, this paper falls short of novelty, clarity, and significance.

content.title: The Importance of Suppressing Complete Reconstruction in Autoencoders for Unsupervised Outlier Detection
content.abstract: Autoencoders are widely used in outlier detection due to their superiority in handling high-dimensional and nonlinear datasets. The reconstruction of any dataset by the autoencoder can be considered as a complex regression process. In regression analysis, outliers can usually be divided into high leverage points and influential points. Although the autoencoder has shown good results for the identification of influential points, there are still some problems when detect high leverage points. Through theoretical derivation, we found that most outliers are detected in the direction corresponding to the worst-recovered principal component, but in the direction of the well-recovered principal components, the anomalies are often ignored. We propose a new loss function which solve the above deficiencies in outlier detection. The core idea of our scheme is that in order to better detect high leverage points, we should suppress the complete reconstruction of the dataset to convert high leverage points into influential points, and it is also necessary to ensure that the differences between the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the original dataset and their corresponding reconstructed results in the direction of each principal component are equal. Besides, we explain the rationality of our scheme through rigorous theoretical derivation. Finally, our experiments on multiple datasets confirm that our scheme significantly improves the accuracy of outlier detection.
